If you would like to have a look at the decision, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 28, which concerns the region of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this decision concern the entire territory of the municipality of Prijedor or only part of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not distinguish within the territory, so it must refer to the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I read this in Serbo-Croat? Could I read part of the decision in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "This assembly of the Serbian people of Prijedor municipality unanimously adopts a decision on the joining of the Serbian territories of the Prijedor municipality to the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is only -- that only Serbian territory is concerned or, rather, that the SDS considered to be Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Serbian territory is not defined in this resolution, and of course, there were claims at times by the SDS that all territories -- all of any municipality in which the Serbs owned a certain percentage of land as Serb territory. Its meaning is, I think, unclear in this context. There were other municipalities in which they enumerated specific villages which were scattered about the municipality, which would join -- or form the Serbian assembly and in some cases subsequently join the ARK. That's not going on here. There's just a blanket statement of Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that the SDS, that its policies were to divide certain municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, having analysed various documents from the binder before you, did you find any references to the Yugoslav People's Army or the VRS or to members of these armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking about this corpus of paper, or this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, this concerns all the documents in the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The two volumes, in other words. Two volumes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which documents you found a reference to the Yugoslav People's Army or the army of Republika Srpska? Or if you like, I could help you or refer to certain documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are probably maybe a hundred references or more in these documents to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But how many documents -- in how many documents was the JNA one of the active participants in the creation of the documents or in the cessation of the assemblies -- in the sessions of the assemblies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not certain what the total number would be. There are two in which either the JNA or VRS plays a, I would say, prominent role.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would any of these documents be a record of the -- of May 12th, 1992, of the -- it is Prosecutor's Exhibit 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us for what reason the military officers attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the meeting at which the decision was passed to create the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that during that assembly, Mr. -- General Mladic held a speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that in his speech, page 41 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Okay, I have page 41 of the 12 May meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is not a sentence, a paragraph, but several pages. Would you agree in that speech, specifically at that page, you can find several sentences where General Mladic took up positions where people of different nationalities could remain within the framework of the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another document which reads -- first to the army of Republika Srpska. It is Exhibit 63. It is an assembly of the Serb people's assembly in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have a translation in English of a small portion of that document, and the Croatian version has about 200 pages. Have you been able to read the whole document in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you conclude from the English extract that it was a meeting where the misunderstandings between the political parties and the army had been very pronounced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. I have got an urgent personal phone call, which I would like to attend to. I will resume the sitting immediately after I finish this phone call. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please, you may be seated. I'm sorry about that, but I have a personal family problem back home today which I have to attend to, and more or less I was expecting this call. And I might have further calls in the course of this morning's hearing. So please bear with me. Please, Ms. Fauveau, carry on with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the report, the last exhibit I referred to was Prosecution Exhibit 52, which is a report of the assembly of Republika Srpska of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you said that you were able to read only the excerpt translated into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I read somewhat further than that but did not master the full 200 pages of the document yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you have analysed the document of 200 pages on the basis of a few excerpts without having read the whole text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't analysed the document. I have cited excerpts from remarks by Dr. Karadzic, which I believe occurred toward the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that during that session of the Republika Srpska assembly, there were declarations that reflected problems between the political and military authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: These problems existed since 1992 until 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to Prosecution Exhibit 19? I think it is up to the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter corrects herself: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Document dated September 13, 1990. Exhibit 19; the English 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that, Prosecution 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the examination, you spoke of an order of the JNA of 1990, according to which the arms of the TO were placed under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You referred to Exhibit 19, Prosecution Exhibit 19.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the author of this document is? I speak of an institution and not of an individual that signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- it's from the -- the document was originated by the TO organisation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a JNA, document, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It refers to the JNA order in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document, the document which this exhibit refers to in its first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, have you seen the original version of this document of Exhibit 19B in the Serbo-Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the researches you have carried out in Bosnia before the war for your book, I suppose you have seen many official Yugoslav documents, originals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the official Yugoslav documents carry a signature and a stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In most situations they do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the last page of this exhibit in the Serbo-Croatian language, and can you tell us whether this exhibit has a stamp and a signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at the end of 1991, Milosevic ordered the JNA to recruit members of the Bosniak nationality in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated that the -- that Borislav Jovic, in his diary, reports that he and Milosevic together rang up the Federal Secretary of Defence, Veljko Kadijevic and that Milosevic directed that he move those JNA troops who were not native Bosnians or citizens of Bosnia to other republics and that those who were citizens of Bosnia serving in the JNA in other republics be transferred to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment? I'd like to ask the -- Mr. Cayley whether this document, document P19A and B, is being contested by the Defence, because I have the vague impression that because of the two stamps that there are on the first page of the Serbo-Croat version this was not objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The -- from memory, Your Honour, to be frank with you, I don't know, but I'm told it was a disputed document originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, it is an objected-to document because the stamp on the first page doesn't prove anything, and there is not a stamp on the signature at the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us suppose that the order of Milosevic had taken place. All citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of their nationality, were transferred to units of the JNA in Bosnia. Muslims, Croats, Yugoslavs, and others had been transferred along with the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In your report, you speak of the functions of the JNA. Can you tell us whether the JNA, in addition to defending the country against external enemy, also had the tasks of defending the territorial integrity of the country of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your examination, you said that the JNA had sided with the Serbs, taking -- taken part with the Serbs in Croatia during the war between the Serbs and Croats in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe my testimony was that it had sided with the Serbs in Croatia during the war in Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the declaration of independence of Croatia constituted an attack against the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not able to make that judgment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the forces of the JNA in Bosnia was increased by the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: What time did the JNA forces retreat from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did some of the JNA forces remain in Croatia until June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Small numbers of JNA troops remained in Croatia until that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a part of the heavy armaments of the JNA remained in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that was part of the agreement of January 2 ending the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the agreement; I'm talking about the heavy weapons that the Croatian forces seized in September and October 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take it your question, then, is, Was I aware that some of the heavy weaponry of the JNA was seized by Croatian forces and retained in Croatia? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've said that the Yugoslav army, that is the JNA, became Serb due to the fact that a large number of officers of different nationalities, Muslims, Croats, Macedonians, left the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a process that -- of which that was one part. It became increasingly Serb over time, first in Croatia, and then somewhat later in Bosnia; that is, in 1992, because of the withdrawal of non-Serbs from that force and the increasing pro-Serb orientation in that force in each place respectively, in Croatia and then Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that with the secession of republics, Slovenia and Croatia, the officers of those nationalities joined their national armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that with the formation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims officers joined the ranks of that army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- are you speaking of 15 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. And again, that's a process that began before that time and accelerated certainly with the formation of the unified command on April 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday of Sefer Halilovic, who became commander of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Sefer Halilovic was a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Sefer Halilovic is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Sefer Halilovic was not a Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't follow the question. Was he a resident or citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that the question? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Sefer Halilovic was born in Sandzak, in the republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Serb army in Bosnia was principally composed of Serbs born in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly by April of 1992, that would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that these Serbs of Bosnia, members of the Bosnian Serb army, were often defending their native towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hard to say how -- whether that would be often the case. I would simply say they were stationed there and were active in the military activities of the army, the JNA; and after May 12th, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in any event, these people were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The vast majority of them were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you referred to Prosecutor's Exhibit P11, which is an extract from the minutes of the second session of the assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina held on the 14th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document refers to a declaration of the minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mahmut Cehajic, who described the Serb people as genocidal. This is Item 8 of the decision. It is discussed on the last page in the last paragraph. Minister Mahmut Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen the speech of Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out investigations to try and trace it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were not aware of the competences of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said I could not comment on the competence of the regional crisis staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you could tell us what were the competences of crisis staffs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How, then, can you provide any document -- can you attribute real significance to any document of a crisis staff? How can you assess it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I, as an historian looking at these things, look at their consequences, their implementation, their impact on events. I am not qualified to give a legal interpretation of those competencies or authorisation as contained either in constitution or statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In history, does an official document have an equal value to an unofficial document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can have, and in fact, many unofficial documents are almost worthless because they are very skeletal in nature and give very little real information. I would say that each document has to be assessed individually in terms of its content and context and origin to make that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question for you. On page 70 of your report, you speak of a Serb sniper who shot at demonstrators on the 6th of April and that that marked -- that some people believe that incident marks the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the identity of the person who fired the shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation on that -- on that day was there was a demonstration of members of all nationalities in front of the national assembly building in downtown Sarajevo, several thousand people, and at a point in time the Holiday Inn, which was then functioning as the headquarters of the SDS, came under fire from Serbian paramilitaries on the roof. So I would probably want to say that this was a member of a Serbian military force. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And as to his nationality, I couldn't give you a definitive statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How can you know that a Muslim or a Croat did not infiltrate himself into the Serb paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't. And furthermore, there were at this time in all these formations small numbers of people who were not from the nationality or the party that controlled it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you allow for the possibility that it may not have been a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Fauveau. It's not over for you yet, Dr. Donia, because I understand Mr. Cayley has a few more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm having fun, Your Honour, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So re-examination by Mr. Cayley. Do you anticipate to finish within the next half hour, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I may, Mr. President. I may go on a bit longer, but I will try and wrap this up as rapidly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have been taking the attitude, as you may have noticed, of interfering as little as possible because I think that would bring us to an end quicker, to tell you the truth. So take that message from me. I will not be interrupting you, but please try to be as concise and as direct as you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, just to orientate you, what I want to do, first of all I want to revisit some of the areas of cross-examination from yesterday and today, and I will refer to the transcript and refresh your memory. I'll summarise what was said to save time so I don't have to read the transcript out, but I will mention the page number to help my learned colleagues opposite. I then want to, lastly, speak about this book by Professor Burg and Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he's listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor Shoup. Dr. Donia, yesterday, Mr. Ackerman raised a point with you where he put to you that the reappearance of Ustasha symbols in the Krajina led to fright and worry amongst people. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then he put to you a question, and this is at page 1205 of the draft transcript:

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In that context, it would not be difficult to understand why people might want to arm themselves for protection, if for no other reason." And your answer to that question was:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't share that conclusion, no. Why do you not share that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't share the conclusion because at this time, that is 1990, early 1991, this was a hypothetical historical -- historically recollected threat from the -- from 45 years beforehand, and the difference between that and an actual armed threat is very great. And so the taking up of arms at this point in time would have been more an act of -- indication of probable use or intent to possibly use them in aggressive purposes rather than defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And who at the time was taking up arms for aggressive purposes rather than defence, Dr. Donia, in the Krajina region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what period of time are we --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The end of 1991, the beginning of 1992. So the summer of 1991 through to the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I've indicated, there was -- each of the three national parties were taking up arms. The increasing flow of arms and link with the JNA was being done by SDS organs and related Bosnian Serb organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can move ahead, you were asked - in fact, there was a lengthy discussion at one point between you and Mr. Ackerman - about the change in the electoral legislation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the passing of legislation which enabled multiparty elections but the prohibition of parties formed on national grounds, and then mention was made of the fact that the constitutional court overturned that condition within the electoral legislation to allow parties to be formed on national grounds. And Dr. Trnka was identified as the Muslim president of the constitutional court at the time. And I sensed an impression was left whereby there was some kind of suggestion that there was a Muslim conspiracy to rig the election laws to allow the formation of nationalist parties. Are you aware of any evidence whatsoever to suggest that there was some form of Muslim agreement to the exclusion of the other nationalities in Bosnia to form parties on a national basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The constitutional court decision, which I can't speak to its validity, but it is a document that, in fact, recognises that there was a danger to formation of political parties along national and religious lines. But the decision reads that these dangers were something that had to be lived with in a democratic society, and that banning parties based on nationality or religion of any type was not consistent either with a constitution or with the rights of the citizens to associate in political groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, when the constitutional court made that decision, were you aware of whether or not there were any Serb judges, Bosnian Serb judges, sitting on that court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the composition of the court at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman asked you a number of questions about the referendum, and here I'm referring to the referendum that was held throughout Bosnia on the question of independence. And you stated, in effect, at page 1256 of the transcript, that you were unaware of any evidence to show that the SDS actively prevented that referendum from taking place. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you turn to page 69 of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I refer you to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you would slowly read out that passage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The SDS urged Serbs to boycott the independence referendum scheduled for 29 February and 1 March. Leaders of the ARK, echoing the official SDS view, declared the referendum to be illegal. They instructed officials of ARK-member municipalities that they were under no obligation to secure voting locations, nor to organise the voting."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So whilst the SDS did not prevent the referendum from taking place, it is true to say that they effectively hijacked it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they relieved the local organs of any responsibility to provide for the voting to take place. And I don't know that I would use the word "hijack," but it was a clear effort to make the voting as minimal as possible and to urge that Serbs not participate in any way within -- in the process of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to very briefly address you on Prosecutor's Exhibit 25. It's not absolutely essential that you have it in front of you, but it may help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, in your cross-examination, you acknowledged that there was discussion and dissension within the SDS in certain quarters regarding these instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In terms of practical application of these instructions in Serb municipalities in the Krajina, by the end of 1992, from what you know, had these instructions been implemented in any of those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had. They had been implemented in nearly all that I know of and have looked at. They were implemented in those municipalities in the ARK by certainly the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you were asked by Mr. Ackerman about the minutes of the ARK assembly that had been provided to you, and you made it quite clear those that had not been provided to you or those that the Prosecutor simply does not possess. But I would, just for the purposes of accuracy in the record, if you could go to footnote 213 in your report which is on page 66.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At footnote 213, can you tell me which session of the ARK Assembly is referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The thirteenth session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were provided with the minutes of the thirteenth session and you in fact referred to them in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could assist me and put that map on an easel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I think you will recall in your evidence yesterday that Mr. Ackerman addressed you about the Muslim authorities in Gorazde and Konjic dismissing Serbs. Now, the first question I have for you is do Gorazde and Konjic constitute part of the Krajina region of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they're both far from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just indicate to the Judges where those two municipalities are so there's absolutely no confusion about the locations of these places in relation to the geography that is of interest to this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gorazde -- may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gorazde is here, east of Sarajevo. Konjic is down here, about halfway between Mostar and Sarajevo. I guess the nearest that -- well, ARK municipalities are considerably further to the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just briefly indicate where the Krajina is? I know we've done this already, but just for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In its broad definition, it would be this north-western third or so of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, it was suggested by inference - and now I'm talking about the Lisbon agreements brokered by Cutilheiro - it was suggested that Izetbegovic essentially prevented those agreements from taking place by his actions. Do you recall that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did both of those failed agreements involve cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did Izetbegovic at that time favour the division of Bosnia along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can briefly move to the respective strengths of Serb forces on the one hand and Muslim and Croat forces on the other, and I'll just remind you of your testimony here. It's at page 1258 of the draft transcript. Forces were referred to by Mr. Ackerman in both Central Bosnia and up in Doboj, and effectively it was put to you that Muslim forces in Doboj were strong enough to hold off Serbian forces. Now, you may not know the answer to this question. If you don't, simply say you don't know. Were you aware, Dr. Donia, that the town of Doboj fell in a day to Serbian forces on the 3rd of May of 1992? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, that area of Doboj, and, in fact, Mr. Ackerman mentioned a speech by Mr. Krajisnik mentioning the Semberija area, that that was of critical importance to the Serbs, the Posavina corridor, in linking areas in northern Bosnia to Serbia proper. Are you aware of the significance of that area of Bosnia for that reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, the -- it was one of the six strategic goals outlined on 12 May, the establishment of a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're running ahead of me, Dr. Donia. We'll get there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, are you aware that by the end of June, by and large the Serbian army had taken control of the Posavina corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've already stated that one of the strategic objectives of the Serbs was the securing of that corridor between Serbian areas in Northern Bosnia and Serbia proper. And if I can refer you now to Prosecutor's Exhibit 50. Page 13 of the minutes of the sixteenth session of the Assembly of the Serbian people held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May. At the bottom of page 13, it states:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there may be a confusion here in the interpretation. I think on Channel 4 now we are receiving interpretation in French, which I can live with, but it's not in English as I had expected. I know that Ms. Fauveau had nothing to do with it. When you think that this fault is rectified, tell me so that we can proceed. I can easily ask you to proceed without having to use it, but I don't know whether we are procedurally correct if there is no interpretation in English. Can we proceed? Okay, so proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Dr. Donia, the second strategic goal at page 13, the corridor between Semberija and Krajina described by Krajisnik as "of the utmost importance to the Serbian people because it integrates the Serbian lands," and so on. I won't read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the speaker here is Dr. Karadzic, not Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're quite right. It starts with Krajisnik and then goes on to Karadzic. So the military action that Mr. Ackerman was addressing to you in terms of the taking of Doboj, the taking of the Posavina Corridor, and the success of that action is actually the fulfilment of this second strategic goal referred to by Karadzic in these minutes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There was a point in your cross-examination yesterday where you were asked about whether or not non-Serb dominated municipalities were asked to join the ZOBK, ARK, and whether there was an initiative on the part of the SDS to do this. And I would like to refer you to page 49 of your report. And you'll find that there is the paragraph that starts "Under the table..." You know what it says; it's your report. But if you could essentially summarise the findings in that part of your report on this particular point that I'm addressing you on now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The effort to recruit other municipalities to the ZOBK continued for some months after it was formed. Among other places, in the official SDS newspaper, Javnost, which issued an invitation and recommendation to municipalities with largely Muslim populations. And then I noted that except for very few Serbian splinter parties, there were no takers among the other political groups to join the ARK -- or to join the ZOBK at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have another about sort of five to ten minutes of re-examination. I don't know whether you wish me to carry on or wish me to pause at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to consult the interpretation room, see whether it would be... Okay. So you can go ahead for the next five, ten minutes, not more than that. Then we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I inquire: In some jurisdictions, I would be permitted a re-cross. I don't know how we're going to handle that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, if you ask for it, I will grant it. Because I think once there is a re-examination, I would concede that. But I would ask you to inform the Chamber beforehand what questions you want to put, see whether they are relevant or not. If it is something which is substantially important, I will let you. If it's not, I will not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, if I can address you on this, this has arisen on other cases before. Mr. Ackerman has had a day and a half to cross-examine this witness. I may then wish to come in after him, if something is raised. I mean, it will go on forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. You won't go forever because that will be the end. He will only be allowed to put any further questions that have arisen out of your re-examination, in other words, any fact that has emerged as a result of your re-examination, and that's it. It will not be a recommencement of the interrogation. But if something comes out of the re-examination, yes, I will allow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will then have an opportunity to do a re-redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, if there is something. But then I will definitely put an end to it. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, this book, "The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina" by Professors Burg and Shoup, now, you were referred to this book on nine different occasions. You probably didn't count them, but you do recall being referred to this publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you will recall that Mr. Ackerman stated -- counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin stated that this book is an authoritative source. Do you recall him stating that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record does not reflect that. What I said was, "Is it an authoritative work?" I asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked the question, and he told you that he doesn't consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you agreed with Mr. Ackerman that this was a work by two well-distinguished American scholars with an impressive work record in regard to the issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could hand out an exhibit, please, Your Honours. This is an extract from chapter 4 which Mr. Ackerman referred to. He didn't refer to this section of chapter 4. I'm going to refer to it now because I think it's important that the Court sees the other conclusions that these authors reached. I have incorporated, Your Honours, as much of the remainder of this chapter as possible, and I will explain to you why after I finish my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have those papers in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I don't intend, Your Honours, to read all of these pages. Do the interpreters have a copy of this? Yes. They do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see, starting in the second paragraph of this document, where it says: "A massive ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me read some of this to the Court: "A massive campaign of ethnic cleansing was initiated by the Bosnian Serbs in April, May, and June 1992 in Eastern Bosnia, parts of Eastern Herzegovina, the Sava River Valley, Bosanska Krajina, and the suburbs of Sarajevo." And the events with which this case is concerned, Dr. Donia, are the events which took place in the Bosanska Krajina, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Carrying on: "These operations were carried out by local militia and SDS activists following the occupation of predominantly Muslim cities by paramilitary forces. As we noted earlier, the paramilitary troops were aided by JNA units from Serbia. The Serb campaign of ethnic cleansing established a pattern that was to be followed on other occasions and by other groups throughout the war but nowhere else on such a large scale. Muslim women and children were usually forced across the battle lines into Bosnian territory or transported out of Bosnia to the Sandzak and even on occasion to Macedonia. Most women and children were spared incarceration and death but were totally at the mercy of their tormenters. As we noted above, many women became the victims of rape." Now, I'm not going to read all of this in. I'm going to select some passages. Another sentence begins: "Men and boys were interned and many were killed outright either upon capture or during incarceration in the worst of the Serb detention camps. In a practice reminiscent of World War II, local political Muslim leaders, teachers, and professionals were selected and executed by the Serbs." And you can see, Dr. Donia, and so it carries on explaining how the intelligentsia were essentially executed. Lastly from this document, on the second page, the last sentence of the first but incomplete paragraph on that page: "The Serbs, furthermore, were guilty of the complete eradication of Muslim cultural monuments, mosques, libraries, and the like in territory under their control. The apparent scorched-earth approach of the Serbs to Muslim cultural and religious structures suggests either a total lack of control by Serb leaders over extremists or an obsession with removing all signs of Muslim presence." Dr. Donia, I will not ask you whether you agree or disagree with professors Burg and Shoup, but I will put it in the manner that Mr. Ackerman put it in some of their statements yesterday. Do you have any quarrel with Burg and Shoup in respect of these conclusions that I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have photocopied a number of pages which don't actually relate to the matter which I've just addressed, and the reason for that is that these pages do speak about Muslims cleansing Croats, Croats cleansing Muslims, Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how we would expected you to do it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think it's only fair that you receive a full picture of what these authors were speaking of when they wrote this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. We would have preferred -- we would have preferred at this point in time to have the book, too, but anyway, have you finished with your --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I've finished my re-examination, Mr. President. The book is in fact in the library here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will definitely consult it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I will put back so that you may use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Have you given your exhibit a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The report of Dr. Donia first, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 53, and I think that this document will have to -- it is actually part of DB1. It's a Defence Exhibit, but I don't know if Mr. Ackerman will want it exhibited in his case. We can call it Prosecutor's Exhibit 53.1, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can live with that. Yes. Now, very briefly, what -- you mentioned that you would like, before you even -- before Mr. Cayley had even started his re-examination, that you may have to -- some questions to put. Do you have questions that you would like to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two things. If the Chamber would like the book, I would be delighted to provide three copies, one for each of you. If you ask me to do that, I will do it without hesitation. The second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber wouldn't accept anything like that. The Chamber will procure its own. Yes, second thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm thinking about is making the entire book an exhibit, not a gift. A gift would not be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. I understand. In that case, you would exhibit one total -- one copy and that's it but as an exhibit. Your second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one question that I would like to ask. It has to do with the events in the corridor. Very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, before -- before things began to fall apart in Bosnia-Herzegovina and war actually broke out, there was no hindrance that would prevent people from the Krajina from driving over to Serbia through the corridor if they wanted to, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the strategic importance of that corridor was not just something that the people in the Krajina were aware of, it was something that the Croatian and Muslim forces were aware of, and that was why it was important to them to try to capture it as quickly as possible to shut off the connection between Krajina and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that that interest was there, but as events evolved, that was not really the way that the military forces behaved in terms of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that during the time the Croatian and Muslim forces had closed the corridor so there could not be any travel and communication back and forth, that a number of babies died in the Banja Luka hospital because oxygen could not be brought from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, here I will stop you because this question you could have put before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's the way it will go. I suppose you don't have questions yourself, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't have any questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so now. That's what I meant. So that you will know what the procedure is, I will be making distinctions between witnesses and witnesses. This is a particular witness. He is an expert witness. And at least my vision of the right of cross-examination would extend to further questioning following re-examination if new facts emerge. In other words, this Chamber will not preclude the Defence or the Prosecution from making further questions. But they have to be justified. This is -- and don't expect this further questioning to last more than a minute or two. Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I just apply for admission into evidence of Prosecutor's Exhibit Number 53, being the report of Dr. Donia, together with 53.1, which is the further extract from the Burg and Shoup publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I ask you to be indulgent with us and instead of having the usual -- how much time do you need, Ms. Korner, after we reconvene? Do you need the full hour?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The video takes something in the region of 25 minutes. But I should be stopping at various points so the investigator can point out the relevant areas. In addition to that, I want to deal with two matters with him that were raised by Mr. Ackerman during the course of cross-examination of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection from anyone that we extend our hearing from quarter to 2.00 until 2.00? Interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will reconvene at 5 minutes past the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to make a formal offer of DB1 into evidence, and I now do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Donia has not been formally released by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. The reason for that is I wanted to discuss with my other two colleagues whether there were any questions. I personally didn't have any questions. Also, he is an expert witness, and I would rather prefer not to go into a direct questioning exercise with him. My two colleagues also don't have any questions, so he can be released now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, and the message will be passed to him. Your Honour, in that case, may I recall Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may. Please call in Mr. Inayat. Everything is ready for the film, for the video recording?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand so. I see Mr. Ackerman is up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've offered Exhibit DB1 but the record doesn't show whether it has been admitted as an exhibit or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I told you. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst Mr. Inayat is coming in, can I explain that we have given to Defence counsel and to Your Honours copies of his annotated schedule of exhibits. Your Honours will see what he has Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. done. This relates to the Banja Luka set of documents, which Your Honours will get back at the end of the day. We have prenumbered those exhibits so that we don't have to go through that rather mind-numbing exercise we did last time. Unfortunately, in doing so, we forgot that some of the exhibits from there had been placed into Dr. Donia's binders, so what we are doing is just leaving the sequence blank and inserting the numbers those documents already have. May I say again, that if required, on Monday, Mr. Inayat, before the first witness, can give -- if there's to be any objection to the admission of those exhibits, can give further evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Inayat, you will now be asked to make the usual solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we have the film shown, can I deal with two matters that arose from cross-examination of Dr. Donia by Mr. Ackerman? He was asked about seeing minutes from the ARK Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, minutes of the ARK Crisis Staff meetings, in other words, records of what was said and who said it, is the Office of the Prosecutor in possession of any such minutes?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: 1998, when we searched the Municipal Assembly building in Banja Luka, that was one of the things that we were trying to look for, and we even asked the local officials who were conducting the tour with us that if they could please take us to where this documentation would be available. We were told in 1992, at the end of 1992 when ARK was disbanded, the officials who were handling that material, they took it with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Since the search took place in Banja Luka, has the Office of the Prosecutor made numbers of attempts through information and other methods to find those minutes?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I think an extensive effort has been made, I would imagine from summer of 1999, that we have been trying to locate this material, even requesting RS officials and sometimes even our own sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In November of last year, was a formal request made through the liaison officer of the Republika Srpska to provide the Office of the Prosecutor with the minutes relating to the ARK Crisis Staff and all the municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct. The request was made on 5th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as yet, has there been any response to that request?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: So far there's been none.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter I want to deal with is this: Mr. Cayley dealt with part of it in cross-examination of Dr. Donia. He was asked whether he had been shown the minutes of the -- he was dealing with the ARK Assembly, not the Crisis Staff, the first, third, fourth, fifth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, thirteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth sessions, and he replied that he had not. Now, have researches been done to establish which sets of minutes the Office of the Prosecutor is actually in possession of?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I was given this information last evening, and I have to point out that so far I have not been able to establish whether we have these or not, although I have tried to look at records. But I can assure you that by Monday morning, you can have my extensive answer on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I'll leave that matter. Then, Your Honour, before I ask for the video to be played, can I hand to Your Honours copies -- Your Honours may have it already, but it's a full map of the ARK area, and it will make it easier to follow. And it may help -- and there's one for the Registry if they require it -- if Your Honours also have the indictment available to you because I shall be pointing out various parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, do you have questions arising or following what -- following the questions that have been put by Ms. Korner to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have -- is there a reaction on your part? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we also need the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, in July of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, in July of last year, using a helicopter, did you personally film part of the area that is covered by this case?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give us the exact date?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I believe it was 22nd of July when we took the helicopter flight, and I believe it was 27th of July, that is, five days after the first helicopter flight we went to Manjaca detention camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we can ask for the video to be played. And, Mr. Inayat, if you can ask for it to be paused where there's some matter you want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that although Mr. Inayat will be pointing out allegations that are made, can I put it that way, he will be pointing out scenes where the Prosecution alleges that there were killings clearly as a matter of proof, but rather than saying each time "alleged," if one can take it as read that's what he would say.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: And before the video is played, Ms. Korner, would you want me to show on the ELMO the route the helicopter took?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Inayat. That would probably be quite helpful. If it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I would suggest, Mr. Inayat, is that while you are showing us the route the helicopter took, you mark it on that same document with a pen or whatever and that that document then will be entered into the records of the case as an exhibit so that we can refer to it later on as a specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll just have to check, because we've pre-numbered the Banja Luka exhibits, so we'll have to check what the right exhibit will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can find a solution for that. We can have it as a Court exhibit, Chamber Exhibit C1. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I'll just use the pointer to show the route that was taken by the helicopter, and then I will use then this marker also to point out and to trace the line of the helicopter route. Your Honours, we on 22nd of July, 2001, we took off from the Banja Luka area in an SFOR helicopter, and we started towards Prijedor, and we started filming the area here which is Omarska village. This is where you will see the first shots on the video. From Omarska, Your Honours, we went to Trnopolje, which is this village here north of this lake, this fishpond that you are looking at. From Trnopolje, Your Honours, we went towards Kozarac using this route, which is about five kilometres north of Trnopolje village. Your Honours, after filming Kozarac, we flew north from Kozarac. There's a road, asphalt metal road about 14 kilometres road to the north where the Benkovac military barracks are located. So we filmed the military barracks also. From there, Your Honours, we flew west towards Prijedor city. And here at this point just before entering Prijedor city is the Keraterm ceramics factory, which was also used as a detention camp during the summer months of 1992. And after filming Keraterm, we flew over Prijedor town to show the government buildings, just one short --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Inayat. Can I interrupt? We're going to go into more detail in the video. If you can show the route without explaining.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Okay. Then I can mark with this. So we flew from Banja Luka. Omarska, this is the first place. Then we went to Trnopolje, second place; Kozarac, third place, Benkovac barracks, west Prijedor, Keraterm, and then we flew west to film this Brdo region of villages, Muslim villages on the west of Prijedor town. From here we entered Sanski Most and filmed the Krings detention camp and also Sanski Most town, and we also filmed Betonirka and some places in Sanski Most. From here we went back to Prijedor. Of course we didn't film until we got back to Prijedor. And we filmed Ljubija football stadium here and then Brisevo, an overwhelmingly Catholic village located south of Prijedor town in Prijedor municipality. From here we again entered Sanski Most and filmed Tomina village, which is -- I'm sorry, Tomina is here. And then we filmed the -- this whole area of Vrhpolje and Rostovo villages. From here we entered Biljani, Your Honours, which is here, and we filmed this village of Biljani. After filming Biljani we headed east to Prhovo which is here, Your Honours. And after filming Prhovo, we entered - Your Honours, I'm sorry I should have gone this way - Kotor Varos. And the first place we filmed in Kotor Varos, Your Honours, is this overwhelmingly Serb village of Grabovica, and we'll show you a school in Grabovica. And from here, Your Honours, we went to Vrcici, the Muslim village here, Vrcici, from where we filmed this whole area. This is where the village of Dabovci and Horvocani are located and also a distant view of Cerkin Brdo and Hanifici. After filming this area, Your Honours, we went to Kotor Varos town and we took footage of three or four places there which we will show you as the video comes up. If you want, I can sign this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been given the number by Ms. Gustin. It would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 446.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Will the Defence make a note of that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just before we leave the map, Mr. Inayat, the second part of the film is on Manjaca. Can you indicate to Their Honours where Manjaca is.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Your Honours, Manjaca is a ground video, not an aerial footage but a ground footage. It is located in this area south of Banja Luka, about I would imagine 40 minutes' drive south of Banja Luka city.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could play the video then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Omarska detention camp located at the former Omarska iron ore mines offices, administration building and some other buildings. If you could stop here just for a second, if you can pause here, Your Honours, the big red building that you see is known as the hangar building. And there's a building to the left -- the other red building that we see at the left-hand corner, bottom left-hand corner, is the administration building. Between the hangar building and the administration building you will see a cemented area which was known as the pista. And in just front of these two buildings was a white building which was referred to as the white house. And you see a fourth building, right top hand corner [sic] which was known as the red building. During the months of May, June, July, and August, several thousands detainees were detained in the hangar building, in the administration building, and those who were considered the most dangerous and extremist were detained in the white house and also on the pista. Let me also just, before we start, also mention that approximately 37 female detainees were also detained here who would work in the administration building during the daytime, in the restaurant, which is the first half of the administration building; and during night-time, detained in the administration building second floor where the interrogations were held during that time. All interrogations were held on the second floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. If we can move on, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will get a good view of the pista, the cemented area I pointed out between the two buildings, red and the administration building. The grassy plot that you see on the right-hand side of the white house is where those who were beaten to death -- this is the administration building. Those beaten to death, their bodies would be thrown on the grassy plot, the right-hand side of the white house. Your Honours, you will also see the open cast quarry, the mine where iron ore was extracted. This is the quarry, Your Honours. And this, Your Honours, is the backside of the big hangar building and the administration building. At the back of the administration building is where all the buses would be stopped before prisoners who were detained would be taken off the buses and put into these areas. Your Honours, we are now moving west of Omarska in the direction of Trnopolje village. In the distance, you can see the fish pond which I also showed you on the map which is located south of the Trnopolje camp. These two places are also connected through a rail line and a road, which we see again. This is a fish pond, Your Honours, located just south of Trnopolje village, maybe 200 metres. And this is a railway line running parallel to the road. Your Honours, at the centre of your screens now you are looking at the white building which was the Trnopolje school, which was turned into a detention area, which was also referred to by the Serbs as -- the Serb authorities as the reception centre. This is where thousands of women --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, I'm going to stop you again. I don't think we need to go into too much detail because we have limited time.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: The grassy area just behind the school is also where detainees were kept. So this, Your Honours, is the Trnopolje detention area. It comprised of a school and a community centre. And this is where also the Red Cross had its headquarters. You will also see a railway line very close to this area from where initially the detainees were deported out of Prijedor. The railway line will be now coming at the bottom of your screens. This, Your Honours. This is the road coming from Omarska. And the road in front of the school is now moving towards Kozara Putevi. I think we can fast forward this for a few seconds here. Okay. This is the Ukrainian orthodox church, and we are heading now in the direction of Kozarac, which I said is about 5 kilometres. This, Your Honours, is Kozarac town. And located very close to it is Kamicani village. We are looking at Kamicani and this is the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road. The old Banja Luka/Prijedor road is also running parallel to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours go to paragraph 38 of the indictment, you will see alleged there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A number of killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- killings in Kozarac and in Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we would like to go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, is the wood factory in Kozarac in the middle of your screens, and the main road, Banja Luka/Prijedor road, just in front of it. Trnopolje is on the side. This, Your Honours, is the orthodox church located in Kozarac. And this is, Your Honours, Kozarac looking north where the Benkovac barracks are located about 12 to 13 kilometres in the north. And the road in the centre of your screens is the road taking us to the Benkovac barracks. This, Your Honours, is the Benkovac barracks where a couple of hundred people were detained starting end of May. Those who were trying to flee the area, ambushed in the forest, and brought here. And detained in the barracks that are to the left-hand side facing the forested area. This location is still in the use of the VRS and the JNA seized it in January of 1992. From here, Your Honours, we'll be flying west towards Prijedor city, and first we'll come to the Keraterm ceramics factory which you see in the middle of your screens, the big building. This one is the Keraterm ceramics factory used as a detention camp in May, June, July, and August. There is a big factory to the right-hand side which you can see here. The offices of Kozara Putevi are at the bottom of your screen. This is where most interrogations were conducted of detainees who were detained in Keraterm. This is the front view of the detention camp, Your Honours, and very soon we will see this metal door that you can see -- maybe we need to stop if you want. This one here is room number 3, the metal door, a small path leading towards it, is room number 3 that you'll hear about during the course of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's listed in paragraph 41.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the fifth item down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, is Prijedor town, southern part of Prijedor town. This is a few kilometres west of Prijedor town, the Brdo region. There are six villages located here vertically north to south. This is the first modern village of the Brdo region called Biscani.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is listed at the bottom of paragraph 38, three from the bottom. From the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is still Biscani, and a view of Agici hamlet in Biscani. From here, Your Honours, we will be flying towards Rizvanovici. This here, Your Honours, is the second village in the Brdo area. And very close to Rizvanovici is the village of Rakovcani which we are looking at right now. This, Your Honours, is Rakovcani. From here, we'll be going towards Hambarine, probably one of the biggest villages in the Brdo region. This is Hambarine Polje, and this is Hambarine centre. The big building that you see at the centre of your screens is where the community centre was located, and they have rebuilt it now. This is the village of Carakovo, Your Honours, located alongside Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Both those villages are mentioned in paragraph 38, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The community centre is now in the middle of your screens, big building. Your Honours, now we are looking south towards Prijedor town. And we show you a bridge called Zeger bridge. So this is, Your Honours, Zeger bridge. This is, Your Honours, in Sanski Most Krings detention camp, formerly an iron works company. It is located 1.5 kilometres from the centre of Sanski Most on the Sanski Most/Bosanska Krupa road, about 125 metres long, 30 metres wide hall. The white building that you see just in front of this hall is the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, all these are listed in the paragraph dealing with the camps. It's paragraph 42, page 21 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A view of Sanski Most football ground and sports hall. This is all of Sanski Most, Your Honours, divided into two parts by the river. This is the new mosque in Sanski Most, and this area is Mahala and Muhici settlements right alongside the river. The multistoried white building that you will see now, which you are looking at the top of your screens, is the Hasan Kikic school with the sports hall in the background. This again, Hasan Kikic school with the orthodox church slightly to its right. The next place we are going to see is, Your Honours, the Betonirka camp, this one, which was the cement processing plant. And there are three garages that I would like to show you, and I believe at a certain point, I'll ask the audiovisual just to pause for a second. If they can pause here. Your Honours, you might see a shed with some vehicles parked under it, and just behind the shed you will see three garages with red coloured doors. These are the three garages of Betonirka plant that I wanted to show you. That's fine, you can continue now. Your Honours, there is a multistoried white building to the left of your screens, with a silver roof. This is a police station. And just behind it is the remand centre facing the football ground, this area. Your Honours, from here we will be going to Ljubija in Prijedor, south of Prijedor. This is the football ground in Ljubija. This is the Ljubija Sanski Most road, and we have exhumed a couple of mass graves here in 1999 and 2001. Your Honours, this is the village Brisevo, southern-most part of Prijedor, overwhelmingly Croat village. All this is Brisevo. You will now see a Catholic church, in the middle of your screen now, built in 1990 and destroyed during the attack in July 2000 -- 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And not rebuilt by the looks of it.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, south of Brisevo, now we're in Sanski Most municipality looking at the settlement of Tomina, which is about 9 to 10 kilometres from Sanski Most town. There is this main road that you can see in the middle of your screens. This is the Sanski Most-Kljuc road, Kljuc further south. Recently we have exhumed mass graves here. Your Honours, very close to Tomina. Within a few kilometres are the settlements of Vrhpolje and Hrustovo. This is still Tomina but now we're moving in the direction of the Vrhpolje. Here you see the Vrhpolje bridge, Your Honours, main Sanski Most-Kljuc road. This is Hrustovo -- sorry, Vrhpolje bridge, and this will be mentioned quite a few times during the course of this trial. You will also see a new cemetery very soon where victims are buried. Those were exhumed in 1996, 1997. This here, Your Honours. Your Honours, now we're looking in the direction of Vrhpolje. We'll go back there once again. This is the settlement of Vrpholje, and on this side of Sana River is Hrustovo. This, Your Honours, is Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the fourth killing listed in paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, now we are flying over Vrhpolje and looking in the direction of the hamlets of Begici and Kenjari, two hamlets that will be mentioned in the trial, very close to Vrhpolje, within kilometres. And while still flying over Vrhpolje, we'll soon see the settlement of Hrustovo. This, Your Honours, to the left-hand side of your screens, there's a mosque in the distance, a minaret, I mean, and this is Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the next killing listed in paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, from here we will be flying to Kljuc municipality and the first place -- we're still looking at Hrustovo. The first place we'll come to is the village of Kenjari, this. You can see the new cemetery here where over 280 people are buried. Those were exhumed from three different sites. This village was attacked on the 10th of July, 1992. Biljani is about, Your Honours, 12 kilometres north-west of Kljuc town. And we are looking at Biljani village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that killing is listed in paragraph 41. That's the fourth one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just in front of this forested area that we see at the bottom of the screen is a barn that will be referred to during the course of this trial, very close to the school building which is now turned into a cemetery. There is a stable that you will see, Your Honour, very soon. We are seeing it right now, but I'll be focusing on it. It's a roofless stable here right in the centre, which will also figure -- come up during the course of the trial.
